 1 IV.     FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS

 2 A.      Background of the Video Privacy Protection Act
 3         15.    VPPA generally prohibits the knowing disclosure of a customer’s video
 4
     rental or sale records without the informed, written consent of the customer in a form
 5

 6 “distinct and separate from any form setting forth other legal or financial

 7 obligations.” 18 U.S.C. § 2710(b)(2)(B)(i). Under the statute, the Court may award

 8
     actual damages (but not less than liquidated damages of $2,500.00 per person),
 9

10 punitive damages, equitable relief and attorney’s fees. Id. at § 2710(c).

11         16.    VPPA was initially passed in 1988 to protect the privacy of individuals’
12
     and their families’ video rental, purchase and viewing data. Prior to its enactment,
13

14 members of the United States Senate warned that “[e]very day Americans are forced

15 to provide to businesses and others personal information without having any control

16
     over where that information goes.” S. Rep. No. 100-599 at 7-8 (1988).
17

18         17.    Senators at the time were particularly troubled by disclosures of records
19 that reveal consumers’ purchases and rentals of videos and other audiovisual

20
     materials. As Senator Patrick Leahy and the late Senator Paul Simon recognized,
21

22 records of this nature offer “a window into our loves, likes, and dislikes,” such that

23 “the trail of information generated by every transaction that is now recorded and

24
     stored in sophisticated record-keeping systems is a new, more subtle and pervasive
25

26 form of surveillance.” S. Rep. No. 100-599 at 7-8 (1988) (statements of Sens. Simon

27 and Leahy, respectively).

28

 1         18.    In proposing the Video and Library Privacy Protection Act, later

 2 codified as VPPA, Senator Leahy stated that “[i]n practical terms our right to privacy

 3
     protects the choice of movies that we watch with our family in our own homes. And
 4

 5 it protects the selection of books that we choose to read.” 134 Cong. Rec. S5399

 6 (May 10, 1988). Thus, the personal nature of such information, and the need to

 7
     protect it from disclosure, is the inspiration of the statute: “[t]hese activities are at

10 interests and our whims. They say a great deal about our dreams and ambitions, our

11

 1 C.      How Masterclass.com Disseminates Digital Subscribers’ Personal
           Viewing Information
 2
           1.     Tracking Pixels
 3

 4         30.    Websites and apps use Facebook’s pixel and SDK to collect

 5 information about user’s devices and activities and send that to Facebook. Facebook

 6
     then uses that information to show the user targeted ads.
 7

 8         31.    The Facebook tracking pixel, also known as a “tag” or “web beacon”

 9 among other names, is an invisible tool that tracks consumers’ actions on Facebook

10
     advertisers’ websites and reports them to Facebook. It is a version of the social
11

12 plugin that gets “rendered” with code from Facebook. To obtain the code for the

13 pixel, the website advertiser tells Facebook which website events it wants to track

14
     (e.g., Video Media) and Facebook returns corresponding Facebook pixel code for
15

16 the advertiser to incorporate into its website.

17         32.    Defendant installed the Facebook tracking pixel, which enables it to
18

19

20 because it benefits financially from the advertising and information services that

21 stem from use of the pixel. The pixel allows Facebook to build detailed profiles

22

23

24 serve them with targeted advertisements.
